Standing about one meter tall, the male bustard can weigh up to 15 kg and is known for its long legs, upright stance, and a striking black crown on its white head. The species is endemic to the Indian subcontinent and prefers dry grasslands and scrublands. Its diet is omnivorous, feeding on insects, small reptiles, and seeds. The bird's low reproductive rate—laying only one egg per year—and preference for open landscapes have made it especially vulnerable to threats such as habitat loss, hunting, and collisions with power lines.

It is a mosaic of private agricultural lands and protected zones, which creates challenges for habitat management but also encourages community participation.

The population of the Great Indian Bustard in Nannaj has significantly declined over the decades. In the 1980s and 1990s, sightings were fairly common, and Nannaj was regarded as a reliable location for observing the bird. However, increasing land use for agriculture, infrastructure development, and grassland degradation led to a sharp drop in numbers. Today, sightings are rare and sporadic. According to recent forest department reports, only one or two individuals are occasionally seen in the area. Conservationists fear that without intervention, the species may disappear from Maharashtra altogether.
